Well, it’s good to meet you too, Doc. I, uh, I guess I'm here because of this thing I've been noticing lately. I spend a good amount of time down at the local art museum these days, just helping out and keeping busy now that I'm not working anymore. It's a great place, really wonderful people. It's a pretty big deal for us, lots of local artists, a whole mapped-out route through the downtown area, so there's a lot of coordination and planning involved.

I mean, they are standing right there, maybe two feet away, and I’ll be looking right at them, making eye contact, nodding along, thinking I'm completely engaged in the conversation. But then... I don't know, it's like a radio station just cuts out to static in my head for a minute. I'll suddenly realize I completely missed the entire middle of what they just said. The beginning is there, the end is there, but the actual meat of the instructions is just gone. 

And then I have to stop them, which is always awkward, and say, "Hey, I'm so sorry, can you run that by me again?" It's getting a bit embarrassing, to be honest with you, having to constantly ask people to repeat themselves when I was looking right at them the whole time. You start to feel like people think you don't care about what they're saying, but I do! I really do. So I figured I should probably come in and talk to somebody about it, just to see what's going on.

Well... you know, Sarah hasn't said anything directly. She's a good girl, she doesn't want to make her old man feel bad, I suppose. But the folks at the museum... that's a little different. I wouldn't say they've sat me down and had an intervention or anything dramatic like that. But, well, I've noticed a shift.

I was standing there, looking at this group of eager faces, and I just couldn't remember where I was going with the story. I had to sort of laugh it off and move to the next piece, but I felt like a fool. 

So, I haven't really volunteered to lead one of those in a while. I just tell them my knees are acting up and I'd rather stay inside at the information desk. It's easier that way. I just don't feel that same confidence anymore, you know? It's like I'm walking on thin ice and I'm just waiting to hear a crack. You could probably hear her from the parking lot. \n\nBut even with her, I'll be listening, and the sound is going into my ears perfectly fine, loud as day, but then... it's like my brain just decides to take a little coffee break. I hear the noise she's making, I can hear the tone of her voice, but the actual words, the meaning of what she's trying to tell me, just completely slips right past me. Lost? Oh, no, definitely not. I've got a built-in compass, always have. Even when I was a kid, growing up over on the east side—before they put the new highway in and tore down half the old neighborhood, mind you—I knew every alley, every shortcut, every dead end. I just took a quick left on Maple, cut through the alley behind the old movie theater—the one that closed down back in '98 and is just sitting there rotting, which is a real shame because they used to have the best popcorn—and I was back on the main road in two minutes flat. 

So, no, getting lost isn't an issue at all. My internal map is perfectly intact. It's just the little things right in front of me that go missing, like my glasses or that tape measure I told you about. Well, depressed... that's a strong word, isn't it? I mean, I was sad, of course. Terribly sad. Arthur was a good man, a fixture in my life. You don't just lose someone you've spent every Tuesday and Thursday with for a decade and not feel a profound sense of loss. I missed him terribly. So, no, not depressed most days. Just... adjusting to a new, quieter normal, I suppose.

Repeat stories? No, no, I don't think so. I mean... well, if you were to ask my sister, Martha—she lives out in Dayton now, moved there back in, oh, it must have been 2004 when her husband got transferred with the tire company, which is a whole other saga let me tell you—she might tell you I tell the same stories over and over. Well, planning... no, I wouldn’t say that’s an issue at all. I haven’t noticed any real change in how I put things together or map things out. I’ve always been a fairly methodical fellow when it comes to knowing what needs doing and in what order. I mean, Arthur was the one with the color-coded spreadsheets, sure, but I still had to organize all the actual logistics for the school groups, making sure the buses had a place to park and the docents were all at their stations. 

And even now, at home, I keep a very tight ship. Take my Wednesday routine, for example. I wake up, make my steel-cut oats—like I mentioned before—and then I have a very specific system for the errands. Hardware store first, because old man Henderson gets his deliveries on Tuesday afternoons, so Wednesday morning is when the shelves are fully stocked with those specific brass screws I like for the birdhouses I build. Then the post office, then the grocer. I write it all down on a little yellow legal pad. Always yellow, the white paper just glares too much in the kitchen light, I find. 

So, no, organizing the steps of a task or planning out my week, that hasn't slipped at all. I still know exactly how to get from A to B to C without getting things muddled. If anything, since Arthur passed, I’ve had to be a bit more rigid about my planning just to make sure the museum tours don’t fall apart without him double-checking my work. I sit down every Sunday evening after dinner—usually just a nice piece of baked cod and some green beans—and I map out the whole week. So the planning part of my brain is working just as well as it did twenty years ago, I assure you. Finances? Oh, no, not at all. My finances are... well, they're quite simple, really, but I keep them in perfect order. I've always been very particular about my money. Help with daily life tasks? Oh, heavens no. No, no, I am completely self-sufficient when it comes to the day-to-day running of the house. I mean, I know I was just saying how the museum folks stepped in with the clipboards and the phone calls, but that’s volunteer work, that’s a different beast entirely. Here at home? Absolutely not. I don't need anyone coming in to cook for me or help me, you know, manage my chores or anything of that sort. 

I still do all my own laundry, for instance. Tuesdays are laundry days. I separate the whites and the darks meticulously, always have. I still use that powdered detergent, the one in the big orange box, because the liquid stuff just gets everywhere and leaves a terrible sticky ring on the washing machine lid. Arthur used to just throw everything in together on whatever temperature the dial was stuck on—drove me absolutely up the wall, bless his heart. But I have my system. And I do my own grocery shopping, I cook my own meals... like that baked cod I mentioned, and I make a wonderful roasted chicken on Sundays with carrots and those little red potatoes, the waxy ones that hold their shape in the oven. 

I keep the house spotless, too. They didn't make a big fuss about it, they just quietly took those responsibilities over. And I have to admit, it stings a little bit. I’ve managed those logistics since 2008! \n\nAnd then... well, there are the art walks. I used to lead the downtown architectural art walks every second Saturday of the month, rain or shine. But lately... I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to. \n\nI’d be standing there in front of a group of fifteen eager people, and I'd realize I'd completely misplaced my telescopic pointer, or I couldn't find the binder with the historical reference photos that I literally just had in my hands two minutes prior. So, I told the board my knees were acting up—which isn't entirely a lie, the damp weather does get to them in the mornings—and I stepped back from leading. It’s a terrible shame. I really do miss it.
